Issued at 1247 PM CDT Sat Oct 31 2026

Through next week (Friday)...

Today and Sunday: Shortwave is analyzed today over the ArkLaTex to
MS River Valley. This is leading to widespread moist isentropic
ascent and overcast conditions across the Gulf Coast states. There
is some uptick in deep moisture (PWs in the 1.3 to 1.6 inch
range) but we are dealing with some dry air pockets (depicted as 
"onion" shape in morning 12Z soundings to areas: 700-500mb layer and
surface to 850mb layer). This will take some seeder-feeder 
mechanisms to moisten the dry air layers aloft, which in turn will
lessen the actual observation of rain early on in the forecast 
period. Based on that, rain chances may be scattered or even 
higher than before, but actually observing rain or any heavier 
downpours, with limited insolation, will be much harder to come 
by. The main takeaway is that even though rain chances are in the 
medium to high chance range (40 to 80 percent), it will take some 
continued and efficient isentropic ascent to overcome some of the 
earlier mentioned failure modes. With such dry antecedent 
conditions and severe to exceptional drought over a large portion 
of the Gulf Coast region, any rain will be helpful. However, not 
anticipating much drought improvement with this rainfall. 

The only areas that convective allowing models (CAMs) indicate 
some heavier downpour potential is the axis of slightly deeper 
moisture projected to advect into southeast MS into the Highway 
45, Highway 98 to Interstate 59 corridors. In this region, CAMs, 
including REFS, HREF and HRRR, indicate some slow moving to 
stationary propagation of rain and storms. This leads to some 
outlook of training convection and heavier totals, potentially in 
excess of 3 to 5 inches in a short period of time. REFS and HREF 
probs of exceeding 5 inches are in the low chance range (20 to 30 
percent) and have trended lower than earlier runs. This would be 
extremely beneficial but in low-lying/urban areas, could cause 
localized flash flooding. Based on that, kept the ongoing HWO 
flash flood threat graphic going with no adjustments. Highs will 
be seasonably warm, some 4 to 10F above (75F to 85F with warmest 
along and south of Interstate 20). 

As the shortwave digs through into this evening, rain chances 
will persist and could impact some evening Halloween outdoor 
activities. With the scattered nature, outdoor plans may still 
proceed without any disruptions. However, have a plan in place if 
rain occurs at your location. As a stronger and deeper shortwave 
ejects east out of the Plains into the Ozarks, the highest rain 
totals and rain coverage (50 to 80 percent) will move in after 
midnight north of Interstate 20 into the Highway 82 corridor. This
will swing through the day Sunday as ridge builds over the Rio 
Grande Valley and into the Gulf Coast states. Rain coverage 
lessens into Sunday afternoon to evening. Highs Sunday will be 
more seasonable in northeast MS while seasonably warm to the 
southwest. Lows tonight and Sunday night will seasonably warm, 
some 12F to 20F above (57F to 65F). Relevant portion of previous 
forecast discussion is below. /DC/

Next week: Shortwave ridging will keep things dry Monday in 
advance of a cold front. Subtropical jet will aid in lee 
cyclogenesis off the Rockies Monday. The corresponding surface 
low will rapidly deepen, drawing moisture northward with storm 
development along its cold front. The front should push through 
our area mainly overnight Tuesday into Wednesday morning and 
progressively weaken as the low lift northward, but there are some
synoptic amplitude/upper low differences between global guidance
(which slows down frontal timing). Both on WXnext2 and Stormnet, 
show low severe probabilities to our west and into far western 
portions of our area. Stormnet lightning probabilities diminish as
the system moves east, suggesting weakening by early Wednesday 
morning. That said, potential secondary low development could 
reinvigorate activity in the southeast Wednesday. As far as severe
potential goes, chances overall look low. Linear storm mode and 
high shear low cape type environment suggest a primary 
wind/tornado risk, which would likely be isolated with greatest 
chances west of I-55 and the river. We may also have to watch for 
a heavy rainfall threat with anomalous PWAT concentrated along the
boundary. Some guidance is showing bullseyes in the west of 2 or 
more inches in a short period. More details will come in future 
forecast updates.

Due to the secondary low development, moisture wrap around lingers, 
so low (15-20%) rain chances continue into Thursday. Additional 
rainfall amounts to generally under a tenth of an inch. The jet 
remains active and persistent moist trajectories may keep isolated 
rain chances around to end the week. /SAS/DC/
